---
title: "California Wildfire Analysis"
author: Ethan Anghelache
output: html_document
---

How much do human factors (population, WUI housing growth, roads) explain where wildfires start in California, and can they predict which counties face rising ignition risk?

```{r}
# Load Libraries
library(RSQLite)  # SQL for Fire Data
library(DBI)
library(sf)       # Spatial Data
library(dplyr)    # Data Wrangling
library(tmap)     # Mapping Visualizations
library(tigris)   # Defining our Region
library(randomForest)  # Machine Learning

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

# Load Data
ca_counties <- counties(state = "CA", cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE)
ca_counties <- st_transform(ca_counties, st_crs(ca_wui))  # see note below

# Fire database (SQL)
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), "data/RDS_SQL/FPA_FOD_20260615.sqlite")

# California WUI blocks (filtered from the national file once, in the Console)
ca_wui <- st_read("data/OtherData/ca_wui.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

# Preview the fire data (SQL)
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, DISCOVERY_DATE, NWCG_CAUSE_CLASSIFICATION,
         FIRE_SIZE, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE, FIPS_NAME
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
  LIMIT 5
")

# Preview the WUI data (key columns only, without the shape data)
head(st_drop_geometry(ca_wui)[, c("BLK20", "fips", "HU2000", "HU2020",
                                  "WUIFLAG2000", "WUIFLAG2020", "VEG2019PC")])

# Preview the counties
head(st_drop_geometry(ca_counties)[, c("NAME", "GEOID", "ALAND")])
```

**Data overview (draft):** This project combines three sources. The FPA FOD fire database
records every reported wildfire in the U.S. from 1992–2024, including where it started, when,
how large it grew, and whether it was human- or lightning-caused; I query it with SQL and keep
only California fires. The SILVIS WUI dataset gives housing counts, wild land vegetation, and
WUI status for every census block in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020, filtered to California's
[X] blocks. County boundaries from the U.S. Census (via `tigris`) tie everything together so
fires and housing can be compared county by county.

## 2. California fires over time

```{r}
fires_year <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, COUNT(*) AS n_fires
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
  GROUP BY FIRE_YEAR
  ORDER BY FIRE_YEAR
")

plot(fires_year$FIRE_YEAR, fires_year$n_fires, type = "b",
     main = "California wildfire ignitions per year",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Number of fires",
     pch = 21, bg = "dodgerblue", col = "black")
```

**Takeaway (draft):** California averages roughly 7,000–9,000 wildfire ignitions per year,
with no clear upward trend from 1992 to 2024. The biggest exception is 2005–2008, peaking at
about 13,400 fires in 2007, though part of this spike may reflect changes in how agencies
reported fires. Since fires have grown more destructive while the number of ignitions has
stayed fairly flat, the more useful question we try to answer is not how many fires start, but where they
start and who starts them.

## 3. Is it us? Human vs. lightning ignitions

```{r}
cause_year <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, NWCG_CAUSE_CLASSIFICATION AS cause, COUNT(*) AS n_fires
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
  GROUP BY FIRE_YEAR, cause
")

human   <- cause_year[cause_year$cause == "Human", ]
natural <- cause_year[cause_year$cause == "Natural", ]
unknown <- cause_year[cause_year$cause == "Missing data/not specified/undetermined", ]

plot(human$FIRE_YEAR, human$n_fires, type = "b",
     ylim = c(0, max(cause_year$n_fires)),
     main = "California wildfire ignitions by cause",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Number of fires",
     pch = 21, bg = "red", col = "black")
lines(natural$FIRE_YEAR, natural$n_fires, type = "b",
      pch = 21, bg = "dodgerblue", col = "black")
lines(unknown$FIRE_YEAR, unknown$n_fires, type = "b",
      pch = 21, bg = "gray70", col = "black")
legend("topright", legend = c("Human", "Lightning", "Unknown"),
       pt.bg = c("red", "dodgerblue", "gray70"), pch = 21)
```

**Takeaway (draft):** Among fires with a known cause, humans start the large majority of
California's wildfires. Human ignitions outnumber lightning ignitions every year from 1992 to
2021, and in 2020, 88.7% of known-cause fires were human-caused. However, the share of fires
with an unknown cause has grown from about 21% in 2015 to 45% in 2020, and above 78% after
2021, likely because many recent cause investigations are incomplete. The apparent decline in
human-caused fires is therefore uncertain, so this project limits cause-based analysis to
2000–2020 and uses total ignitions for modeling.
## 4. Ignition density by county

```{r}
# Pull California fires from 2000–2020 (SQL)
ca_fires <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, NWCG_CAUSE_CLASSIFICATION AS cause,
         FIRE_SIZE, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
    AND FIRE_YEAR BETWEEN 2000 AND 2020
")

# Turn coordinates into map points, then match each fire to its county
fires_sf <- st_as_sf(ca_fires, coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4269)
fires_sf <- st_transform(fires_sf, st_crs(ca_counties))
fires_sf <- st_join(fires_sf, ca_counties[, c("GEOID", "NAME")])

nrow(fires_sf)
```

```{r}
county_fires <- fires_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(GEOID)) |>              # drop any points that fell offshore
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(n_total   = n(),
            n_human   = sum(cause == "Human"),
            n_natural = sum(cause == "Natural"))

# Join counts to county shapes and calculate fires per 100 km² per year
n_years <- 21  # 2000–2020

ca_counties <- ca_counties |>
  left_join(county_fires, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(area_km2        = ALAND / 1e6,
         human_density   = round(n_human   / area_km2 * 100 / n_years, 3),
         natural_density = round(n_natural / area_km2 * 100 / n_years, 3),
         human_share     = round(n_human / n_total, 3))
```

```{r}
ca_counties |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(human_density)) |>
  select(NAME, n_human, n_natural, human_density, natural_density, human_share) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
tm_shape(ca_counties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("human_density", "natural_density"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Fires per 100 km² per year")) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Human-caused", "Lightning-caused"))
```

**Takeaway (draft):** From 2000–2020, 184,585 California wildfires were matched to counties.
The highest human-caused ignition densities are in the Bay Area (San Francisco, Santa Cruz,
Contra Costa) and Sierra Nevada foothill counties such as El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, and
Butte, which are areas where homes spread into dry, wooded land. Lightning fires show almost
the opposite pattern, concentrating in remote northern and high Sierra counties. Human
ignition densities also run far higher, reaching 7.207 fires per 100 km² per year compared to
a maximum of 1.499 for lightning. San Francisco's top ranking should be read with caution,
since its small area means relatively few fires (183) produce a high density.

## 5. WUI housing growth by county
```{r}
# Total WUI housing per county, 2000 vs. 2020
county_wui <- ca_wui |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(GEOID = substr(BLK20, 1, 5)) |>
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(wui_hu_2000 = sum(HU2000[WUIFLAG2000 > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
            wui_hu_2020 = sum(HU2020[WUIFLAG2020 > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
            veg_pct     = mean(VEG2019PC, na.rm = TRUE))

head(county_wui)
```

```{r}
#Growth and join to counties
ca_counties <- ca_counties |>
  left_join(county_wui, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(wui_growth_pct = round((wui_hu_2020 - wui_hu_2000) / wui_hu_2000 * 100, 3),
         wui_new_units  = wui_hu_2020 - wui_hu_2000)

ca_counties |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(wui_growth_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, wui_hu_2000, wui_hu_2020, wui_new_units, wui_growth_pct) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
#Map it
tm_shape(ca_counties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "wui_growth_pct",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.purples"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "WUI housing growth (%), 2000–2020"))


```

**Takeaway (draft):** From 2000–2020, WUI housing grew most in the Central Valley, Sierra
Nevada foothills, and Southern California. By percentage, San Joaquin (347.670%) and
Stanislaus (221.065%) grew fastest, but from very small starting points; by number of new
homes, Riverside added the most (165,083), followed by Orange, Sacramento, and Placer. Placer,
Merced, and El Dorado rank in the top 10 for both WUI growth and human ignition density,
suggesting these counties combine frequent human-caused fires with a rapidly growing number of
homes at the wildland edge. Some northern and desert counties saw little growth or even
declines in WUI housing.

## 6 Which counties face rising risk?

```{r}
#Build both measures and classify counties
ca_counties <- ca_counties |>
  mutate(total_density      = round(n_total / area_km2 * 100 / n_years, 3),
         wui_growth_density = round(wui_new_units / area_km2 * 100, 3),
         ign_rank           = round(percent_rank(total_density), 3),
         wui_rank           = round(percent_rank(wui_growth_density), 3),
         risk_group = case_when(
           ign_rank >= 0.5 & wui_rank >= 0.5 ~ "Rising risk",
           ign_rank >= 0.5                   ~ "Fire-prone, slow growth",
           wui_rank >= 0.5                   ~ "Growing, fewer fires",
           TRUE                              ~ "Lower concern"),
         risk_group = factor(risk_group,
                             levels = c("Rising risk", "Fire-prone, slow growth",
                                        "Growing, fewer fires", "Lower concern")))

table(ca_counties$risk_group)
```

```{r}
#Quadrant plots
group_cols <- c("red", "orange", "mediumpurple", "gray70")
pt_cols <- group_cols[as.numeric(ca_counties$risk_group)]

plot(ca_counties$wui_rank, ca_counties$ign_rank,
     main = "Ignition density vs. WUI housing growth by county",
     xlab = "WUI housing growth (rank, 0 = lowest, 1 = highest)",
     ylab = "Ignition density (rank, 0 = lowest, 1 = highest)",
     pch = 21, bg = pt_cols, col = "black", cex = 1.3)
abline(h = 0.5, v = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray40")

rising <- ca_counties$risk_group == "Rising risk"
text(ca_counties$wui_rank[rising], ca_counties$ign_rank[rising],
     labels = ca_counties$NAME[rising], pos = 3, cex = 0.6)

legend("bottomright", legend = levels(ca_counties$risk_group),
       pt.bg = group_cols, pch = 21, cex = 0.7)
```
```{r}
#Map the 4 groups
tm_shape(ca_counties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "risk_group",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = group_cols),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "County risk group"))
```

```{r}
#The rising-risk counties
ca_counties |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(risk_group == "Rising risk") |>
  mutate(combined_rank = round(ign_rank + wui_rank, 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(combined_rank)) |>
  select(NAME, total_density, wui_growth_density, ign_rank, wui_rank, combined_rank)

```

```{r}
cor.test(ca_counties$total_density, ca_counties$wui_growth_density,
         method = "spearman")
```
**Takeaway (draft):** WUI housing growth and ignition density are positively correlated
across California counties (Spearman's rho = 0.553, p < 0.001): counties adding more homes at
the wildland edge also tend to have more fires per area. Most counties fall high or low on
both measures, with 22 of 58 in the "Rising risk" group, 22 in "Lower concern," and only 14
mixed. Rising-risk counties form two belts: one from the Bay Area through Sacramento into the
Sierra Nevada foothills, and one across Southern California (Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside,
and San Diego). Contra Costa, Placer, and Alameda rank highest on both measures combined; San
Francisco technically ranks first, but its very small area inflates both densities, so it is
not a realistic wildfire hotspot. This correlation shows the two patterns overlap, not that
housing growth causes fires.

## 7 Predicting Ignition Density
```{r}
#Housing per county for each decade
county_housing <- ca_wui |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(GEOID = substr(BLK20, 1, 5)) |>
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(hu_2000  = sum(HU2000, na.rm = TRUE),
            hu_2010  = sum(HU2010, na.rm = TRUE),
            hu_2020  = sum(HU2020, na.rm = TRUE),
            wui_2000 = sum(HU2000[WUIFLAG2000 > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
            wui_2010 = sum(HU2010[WUIFLAG2010 > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
            wui_2020 = sum(HU2020[WUIFLAG2020 > 0], na.rm = TRUE))
```


```{r}
#Road length per county
ca_roads <- primary_secondary_roads(state = "CA", progress_bar = FALSE) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(ca_counties))

road_pieces <- st_intersection(ca_roads, ca_counties[, "GEOID"])
road_pieces$length_km <- as.numeric(st_length(road_pieces)) / 1000

county_roads <- road_pieces |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(road_km = sum(length_km))
```
```{r}
#Building county-year dataset
# Fires per county per year
fires_cy <- fires_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(GEOID)) |>
  count(GEOID, FIRE_YEAR, name = "n_fires")

# County features that don't change by year
county_static <- ca_counties |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, area_km2, veg_pct) |>
  left_join(county_housing, by = "GEOID") |>
  left_join(county_roads, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(road_km = ifelse(is.na(road_km), 0, road_km))

# One row per county per year
panel <- expand.grid(GEOID = ca_counties$GEOID, year = 2000:2020,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  left_join(fires_cy, by = c("GEOID", "year" = "FIRE_YEAR")) |>
  left_join(county_static, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(n_fires = ifelse(is.na(n_fires), 0, n_fires),
         # Fill in housing between census years
         hu  = ifelse(year <= 2010,
                      hu_2000 + (hu_2010 - hu_2000) * (year - 2000) / 10,
                      hu_2010 + (hu_2020 - hu_2010) * (year - 2010) / 10),
         wui = ifelse(year <= 2010,
                      wui_2000 + (wui_2010 - wui_2000) * (year - 2000) / 10,
                      wui_2010 + (wui_2020 - wui_2010) * (year - 2010) / 10),
         # Everything per 100 km² so big and small counties compare fairly
         ign_density     = n_fires / area_km2 * 100,
         housing_density = hu / area_km2 * 100,
         wui_density     = wui / area_km2 * 100,
         wui_share       = wui / hu,
         road_density    = road_km / area_km2 * 100) |>
  filter(NAME != "San Francisco")

nrow(panel)
```
```{r}
#Train on 2000-2015, test on 2016-2020
train <- panel[panel$year <= 2015, ]
test  <- panel[panel$year >  2015, ]

f <- ign_density ~ housing_density + wui_density + wui_share + road_density + veg_pct

# Baseline: linear regression
lm_fit <- lm(f, data = train)
summary(lm_fit)

# Machine learning: random forest
set.seed(124)
rf_fit <- randomForest(f, data = train, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
rf_fit
```

```{r}
#Compare models on the test years
rmse <- function(actual, pred) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))
r2   <- function(actual, pred) 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)

lm_pred <- predict(lm_fit, test)
rf_pred <- predict(rf_fit, test)

data.frame(Model = c("Linear regression", "Random forest"),
           RMSE  = round(c(rmse(test$ign_density, lm_pred),
                           rmse(test$ign_density, rf_pred)), 3),
           R2    = round(c(r2(test$ign_density, lm_pred),
                           r2(test$ign_density, rf_pred)), 3))
```
```{r}
#Which features matter? Human vs. natural
imp <- sort(importance(rf_fit)[, "%IncMSE"])
imp_cols <- ifelse(names(imp) == "veg_pct", "dodgerblue", "red")

par(mar = c(5, 9, 4, 2))
barplot(imp, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = imp_cols, border = "black",
        main = "Random forest variable importance",
        xlab = "Increase in prediction error when removed (%)")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Human", "Natural"),
       fill = c("red", "dodgerblue"), cex = 0.8)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))
```
```{r}
#Predicted vs. Actual
plot(test$ign_density, rf_pred,
     main = "Random forest: predicted vs. actual (2016–2020)",
     xlab = "Actual ignition density", ylab = "Predicted ignition density",
     pch = 21, bg = "dodgerblue", col = "black")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

**Takeaway (draft):** A random forest predicted 2016–2020 county ignition density better than
linear regression (R² = 0.430 vs. 0.255; RMSE = 1.821 vs. 2.082 fires per 100 km²). Wildland
vegetation was the single most important feature, but the four human features (WUI housing
density, WUI share, housing density, and road density) ranked close behind and together
carried most of the model's predictive power. In the linear model, WUI housing density was
the only strong predictor: each additional 1,000 WUI homes per 100 km² was associated with
about 0.423 more ignitions per 100 km² per year. Together, these results suggest wildfires
start where people and fuel meet, not from either alone. The model underpredicts extreme
years, likely because it includes no weather or drought data, and its training accuracy
(75.51%) is higher than its test accuracy because counties repeat across years, so the test
R² is the more reliable measure.
